## Peri-Met Study: peripheral metaraminol in septic shock

:::: {.justify}

Septic shock is a life-threatening complication of infection
in which blood pressure falls dangerously low. Treatment
often includes medicines called vasopressors, which raise
blood pressure by narrowing the blood vessels. Increasingly,
these are started through a standard drip in the arm rather
than waiting for a larger "central" line to be placed.

In the UK, the medicine most often used this way is
metaraminol. International guidelines recommend a different
drug, noradrenaline, and the two have never been compared
directly in a clinical trial in septic shock.

The Peri-Met Study aims to address this gap. We are first
reviewing the published evidence, and will use this to
inform on whether or not a small pilot trial at the
Whittington Hospital would be appropriate. The pilot will
test whether a larger, multicentre trial is feasible.

::::
